newsitem.title: DUBAI: Patriot missiles arrive in Saudi Arabia.
newsitem.headline: Patriot missiles arrive in Saudi Arabia.

text.p: Two Patriot anti-missile batteries and U.S. soldiers to operate them have arrived in Saudi Arabia in response to the latest tensions with Iraq, a U.S. military official said on Tuesday.

"The new Patriot batteries ordered into the theatre are in country. They arrived two days ago along with about 170 people," said Lieutenant-Colonel Andrew Bourland, Public Affairs Director for the Joint Task Force Southwest Asia.
"They were sent here in light of the latest tensions with Iraq," he told Reuters by telephone from Riyadh.
The batteries were sent after Iraq fired missiles at U.S. warplanes last week in the latest military confrontation between Washington and Baghdad.
Bourland would not say where the Patriots were being deployed in the kingdom, which served as the launch pad for the 1991 Gulf War that liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.
Patriot missiles were used during the war as defence against Iraqi Scud missiles.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry met Saudi King Fahd over the weekend on a mission aimed at mustering Gulf Arab support for a possible military showdown with Iraq.
The kingdom, Washington's chief strategic ally in the Gulf, has distanced itself from the latest U.S. military action against Iraq.
Defence Minister Prince Sultan said last week that, if asked, Saudi Arabia would have refused to give the United States access to its bases for recent missile strikes against Iraq.
On Sunday he said there were no U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia. American military personnel in the kingdom were tied to United Nations resolutions, he said.

The remarks underscored deep sensitivities in the kingdom, where two bombs killed 24 Americans and two Indians in the last year and militant Moslems oppose the American presence in the birthplace of Islam.

The 170 U.S. soldiers who will operate the Patriot missiles joined 5,000 U.S. military personnel already in the kingdom enforcing the no-fly zone over southern Iraq, part of Operation Southern Watch run by the United States, Britain and France.

The U.S. military has moved most of its personnel in the kingdom to a desert airbase at al-Kharj, 60 miles (100 km) southeast of Riyadh, following a fuel truck bomb that killed 19 U.S. airmen near Dhahran, eastern Saudi Arabia, in June.
Bourland said the move would be completed in a few weeks.
A Pentagon report on Monday said commanders failed to provide adequate protection for the Dhahran post despite evidence that it had become "a potential terrorist target".
Bourland said the U.S. military has already begun boosting security measures to implement the report's recommendations, stressing that "security efforts are continuing."
Tensions between the United States and Iraq, meanwhile, seemed to have eased and Bourland said there were no signs of Iraqi violations in the southern no-fly zone.
"There has been very little Iraqi movement and no radar activity in the last 24 hours," he said.
